land.text: the Lake Petén Itzá region, inside Cliopatria's Later Mayan City-States shape from 1450 to 1546

predecessors.note: The Itza arrived from Mayapan (Nojpetén page: 'fled south around 1441–1446'); Cliopatria's own Itza row only starts in 1547, when the Later Mayan City-States row ends.

land.text: the Itza kingdom around Lake Petén Itzá, taken when 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697'

successors.note: Cliopatria keeps the Itza row to 1699; the Spanish took the land in March 1697.

capitals.name: Nojpetén (Tayasal; Flores)
capitals.note: Island city on Lake Petén Itzá: 'the capital city of the Itza Maya kingdom of Petén Itzá'; renamed Flores in 1831 (coordinates from the gazetteer's Tayasal entry).

correction.text: the shape Cliopatria draws from 1547 (Lake Petén Itzá and the central Petén lakes), used for 1441-1546 because the pages give no boundary: 'settling around Lake Petén Itzá where they remained independent until 1697'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Itza row begins in 1547, but the Nojpetén page dates the Itza move to Lake Petén Itzá to 'around 1441–1446'. Until 1546 Cliopatria draws the lake region inside the Later Mayan City-States shape (1450-1546); the renderer should let this smaller state overlay it. Area from the 1547 shape (33,237 km2); the Itza people page's 'empire covered 230,000 square kilometers, organised into 4 main kingdoms' (about 1519) is seven times larger and is not used (see the 1547 note).

33,237 km2. Starts in 1547 only because Cliopatria's Later Mayan City-States row ends in 1546; the Spanish conquest of Yucatán page confirms Petén stayed outside: 'The polities of Petén in the south remained independent and received many refugees fleeing from Spanish jurisdiction.' Size check: the Itza people page gives 230,000 km2 for the 'Itza empire' of about 1519, 7 times Cliopatria's figure, but the conquest page measures the central lake basin at only 'approximately 100 kilometres east–west by 30 kilometres north–south' and says the Itza 'controlled or influenced much of Petén and parts of Belize'; 33,000 km2 is the more credible reading and the shape is kept.

32,873 km2, 1 percent below the 1547 shape; no event in the pages explains the difference and it does not matter at this resolution. 'Before their defeat in 1697 the Itza controlled or influenced much of Petén and parts of Belize.'

22,346 km2: Cliopatria drops the eastern strip (east of 89.03 W, towards Belize). The pages are silent on a change in 1670 (ledger: loss at confidence 1). The conquest page says the Yalain, Itza allies, held land 'from the east shore of Lake Petén Itzá eastwards to Tipuj in Belize', so the sphere of influence reached further east than this shape; the shape is kept as the Itza proper.

correction.text: the same shape, valid 1696 to 13 March 1697 only; the Itza submitted to Martín de Ursúa's force on 13 March 1697

keyframe_review.note: Shape unchanged (22,346 km2) but the years end in 1697, not 1699: 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697'. 1698-1699 belong to the Spanish Empire.

region.text: the island city Nojpetén (Tayasal) on Lake Petén Itzá and the lake region around it

ledger.note: 1441: the Itza, expelled from Mayapan, settle Lake Petén Itzá and build Nojpetén. 'Ethnohistoric documents claim the founding of Nojpetén in the mid-15th century AD' and the Itza 'fled south around 1441–1446, after they were deposed by the Xiu Maya at Mayapan'; the Itza people page has them 'settling around Lake Petén Itzá where they remained independent until 1697'. The year is the start of the page's range; the pages give the city, not a boundary.

region.text: the eastern strip of the 1564-1669 shape that Cliopatria drops in 1670 (about 10,500 km2, east of 89.03 W)

ledger.note: 1670: page silent. Cliopatria's Itza shape shrinks from 32,873 to 22,346 km2, losing its eastern strip towards Belize; the Spanish conquest of Petén page gives no date for this and says the Yalain (Itza allies) held land 'eastwards to Tipuj in Belize'. Recorded as a bridge, with 'nobody' as counterpart because no state is named for the strip.

region.text: Petén, from the Kejache country north of the lakes where the Spanish road and garrisons stood, towards Lake Petén Itzá

ledger.note: 1695: Spanish troops hold ground on the northern edge of the Itza sphere. 'By November Tzuktokʼ was garrisoned with 86 soldiers and more at Chuntuki' and 'by October Spanish soldiers had established themselves near the source of the San Pedro River'; the Kejache lay 'to the north of the Itza, between the lakes and what is now Campeche'. The page names the garrisons, not a boundary, so the zone is the whole Petén shape.
13 March 1697: the fighting ends with the fall of Nojpetén ('resulted in the final defeat of the independent kingdoms of central Petén').

region.text: the Itza kingdom around Lake Petén Itzá, the capital Nojpetén and the Itza lands

ledger.note: 13 March 1697: Nojpetén falls and the last independent Maya kingdom ends. 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697, more than 150 years after the conquest of the rest of the' Maya; 'On March 13, 1697, the Itza kingdom finally submitted to Spanish rule, represented by a force led by Martín de Ursua, governor of Yucatán' (Itza people page). The Nojpetén page dates the all-out assault itself to 10 March.

wars.name: Mirones expedition against the Itza
wars.outcome: The Itza won: 'on 27 January 1624, an Itza war party led by AjKʼin Pʼol caught Mirones and his soldiers off guard'. 'These events ended all Spanish attempts to contact the Itza until 1695.'
wars.note: Ordered in March 1622 by the governor Diego de Cárdenas; the Spanish got no further than Sakalum, southwest of Bacalar, so no ground changed hands. It follows the Franciscan peaceful missions of 1618-1619.

wars.name: Spanish conquest of Petén
wars.outcome: Spanish victory: road building from Yucatán in 1695, missionary visits in 1696, and the assault on Nojpetén in March 1697 ended the last independent Maya kingdom.
wars.note: The page dates the first Franciscan approach to 1618; the military phase that held ground is 1695-1697. Guatemalan columns from Cahabón (March 1695) withdrew. The Kowoj, hostile to the Itza, were also defeated in 1697 (no detail on the page).

certainty.note: The Itza sphere ('much of Petén and parts of Belize') is approximate throughout; only the island capital and the lake shore are firm.

notes: Itza kingdom: start moved to 1441 (the Nojpetén page's 'around 1441–1446') although Cliopatria's row begins in 1547; between 1450 and 1546 Cliopatria's Later Mayan City-States shape also covers the Petén lakes, so the renderer should draw the Itza core over it. The end is March 1697, not Cliopatria's 1699. Cortés crossed the Itza kingdom in March 1525 (Spanish conquest of Petén page: 'They arrived at the north shore of Lake Petén Itzá on 13 March 1525'; the Itza people page dates his visit to 1523) but nothing territorial happened. The Itza people page's 'empire covered 230,000 square kilometers, organised into 4 main kingdoms' is not credible against the conquest page's measurements and was not used. Neighbours that have no dossier: Kowoj (eastern lakes, hostile to the Itza), Yalain (east shore of Lake Petén Itzá to Tipuj, Belize; Itza allies), Kejache (north of the lakes), Mopan and Chinamita (southeast Petén), Manche Ch'ol (extreme south, under Verapaz administration from 1628), Lakandon Ch'ol (Usumacinta tributaries): see counterparts_needing_dossiers. The 1670 contraction of Cliopatria's shape is not explained by any page opened; a gap-filler could open the Belize/British Honduras history. Year 1525 Cortés and the 1618-1619 Franciscan missions are not ledger events because no border moved.
